rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2014> the authors develop a software tool, run 600 randomly generated hydrant configurations for the Sinistra Ofanto district at 1,200 and 600 l/s, test flow regulators at the Politecnico di Bari hydraulics laboratory, measure Agros 40 sprinkler distribution patterns at Albacete, and size four on-farm sprinkler designs with Labye's method (Figs. 3, 4, 6-10).
rows.notes: The study does not report its own result on the investment cost of on-demand distribution networks. Its cost finding (Fig. 8; Results) concerns the pipe cost of an on-farm solid-set sprinkler sector designed at different upstream hydrant pressures: the design for low pressure (D24) was 38% dearer than D34 but never failed across all simulated hydrant pressures, whereas cheaper small-pipe designs (D49, D55) failed at peak demand. This is a trade-off for the on-farm network under an on-demand supply, not a comparison of on-demand network investment cost with other distribution arrangements, and the claimed causal link (higher network cost because supply is guaranteed at peak) is not tested. In addition, the cost/failure results come from hydraulic simulation of the distribution system and on-farm network whose outputs are not compared with measurements from the real system; laboratory tests on regulators and sprinklers are inputs, not validation. The authors themselves note results are very specific to the case study (Results, last paragraph) and that wind was neglected (Conclusions), but these are not limitations on the claimed effect since Q2 is no.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a methodological/simulation case study (one district, one hydrant, one sprinkler sector) in Apulia, Italy; no field validation of the distribution-system or on-farm performance outputs is reported.
